'''''Bauhinia galpinii''''' is a species of [[shrub]] in the family [[Fabaceae]]. It is [[Endemism|endemic]] to parts of eastern and southern Africa. The species name commemorates [[Ernest Edward Galpin|E. E. Galpin]], a South African botanist and banker. Its common names include '''South African orchid bush''', '''red bauhinia''' and '''Nasturtium bush'''.<ref>[https://www.gardensonline.com.au/gardenshed/plantfinder/show_960.aspx Bauhinia galpinii] GardensOnline Shopping Pty. Ltd.</ref>

It is native to Angola, to Mozambique, Zimbabwe, [[Eswatini]], and to [[KwaZulu Natal]] and the [[Northern Provinces]] of South Africa.<ref name = powo>[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:481322-1 ''Bauhinia galpinii'' N.E.Br.] ''[[Plants of the World Online]]''. Retrieved 30 September 2023.</ref>

==Description==
The leaves are bilobed, each having a symmetrical pair of rounded lobes joined symmetrically about a midrib, with a small, soft [[mucro]]nule in the notch at the tip. The resulting shape gave rise to the [[Afrikaans]] popular name "kameelpoot", meaning "camel's foot". The mucronule is fragile and frequently is missing as a result of minor damage. The flowers in the wild generally are a handsome brick red, but some [[cultivar]]s have pink or orange-red flowers.

==Habit==
The plant is evergreen, with its main growing season in summer. It usually takes the form of a dense, sprawling shrub of up to some {{convert|3|m|ft|abbr=on}} high, but under some conditions, such as in undergrowth, may reach double that height.<ref name="WykWyk2007">{{cite book |author1=Braam van Wyk |author2=Piet Van Wyk |title=How to Identify Trees in Southern Africa |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9HOmOElZL6IC&pg=PA128 |access-date=30 April 2013 |date=July 2007 |publisher=Struik |isbn=978-1-77007-240-4 |pages=128–}}</ref>

==Ecology and uses==
Its flowers are of value to pollinators, including birds, and the sheltering shrubby habit renders it popular as a nesting site for small birds. Sheep and goats can safely browse the leaves and twigs.<ref name= "WattPP">Watt, John Mitchell; Breyer-Brandwijk, Maria Gerdina: The Medicinal and Poisonous Plants of Southern and Eastern Africa 2nd ed Pub. E & S Livingstone 1962</ref>

==Cultivation==
The species is widely cultivated as a fairly [[Drought tolerance|drought-hardy, non-xerophytic]] ornamental in the warm zones of the United States and Mexico where it has [[escaped plant|escaped cultivation]] and [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in some locations, but without any significant tendency towards [[Invasive species|invasiveness]].
